JPMorgan posts surprise drop in fixed-income trading revenue
article:
(Oct 13): JPMorgan Chase & Co reported a surprise drop in fixed-income trading revenue in the third quarter, the first such decline in more than two years.

The fixed-income haul fell 4% from a year earlier, according to a statement Tuesday, a decline that chief financial officer Jeremy Barnum said was part of the “normal course” of ups and downs. Total trading revenue was US$10.3 billion ($13.18 billion) for the period, while analysts were expecting US$10.5 billion.

Still, shares of the company erased earlier losses after JPMorgan said it now expects to earn about US$106.2 billion in net interest income this year, more than the roughly US$105.5 billion it predicted in July, and that its “central case” for next year is about US$107 billion in NII excluding its markets business. Both figures are ahead of analysts’ estimates.

The shares advanced 1.4% to US$338.89 at 9.36am in New York, boosting this year’s gain to 5.1%.

JPMorgan kicked off third-quarter bank earnings Tuesday alongside Goldman Sachs Group Inc, Citigroup Inc and Wells Fargo & Co, with Bank of America Corp and Morgan Stanley slated for Wednesday.

See also: Singapore bank shares tumble as yield surge threatens earnings

Wall Street trading desks are facing fallout from rising interest rates, after the Federal Reserve raised its benchmark rate in September to contain inflation and 10-year Treasury yields approached the highest level in almost a quarter century earlier this month. Higher yields push down the value of existing debt, which can crimp demand for trading services but boost revenue from lending businesses.

“Large fiscal deficits, sticky inflation, elevated asset prices, rising interest rates and geopolitical conditions continue to shift under the surface,” chief executive officer Jamie Dimon said in the statement. “These forces may be manageable, but we remain prepared for a wide range of outcomes.”

Within the fixed-income business, the revenue drop was driven by declines in commodities, rates, credit and public finance, according to a company presentation. That was largely offset by gains from currencies and emerging markets.

See also: UOB launches online branch appointment booking system for over 25 services

The 15% climb in total trading revenue and 14% jump in investment-banking fees came in at the lower end of the range the firm telegraphed at an industry conference last month. At the time, JPMorgan saw both rising by a percentage in the mid to high teens.

Even so, stock traders notched their best third quarter on record, with a 49% jump from a year earlier to US$4.95 billion. That came in ahead of expectations and marked the latest in a series of bumper quarters for that business.

JPMorgan’s investment-banking fees were US$3 billion for the quarter, in line with expectations. Fees from advising on mergers and acquisitions beat estimates, while those for equity and debt underwriting fell short. Dimon said on Bloomberg Television last week that there was “a little bit of a slowdown in September” for the investment-banking business.

The results also included US$658 million of net investment securities losses that Dimon called “discretionary” in the statement.

JPMorgan’s NII for the third quarter came in at US$27 billion, above estimates. Expenses for the quarter were US$27.3 billion, more than expected, and the bank lifted its full-year adjusted expense guidance to about US$108.6 billion, above the US$107.5 billion executives expected in July.

The firm increased its pile of money set aside for potentially soured loans by US$539 million. That reserve build was primarily tied to the wholesale business and “predominantly driven by net lending activity and changes in the credit quality of certain exposures”, according to the statement.

title: Long-term Treasuries hold gains as oil snaps three-day rally
article:
(Oct 13): Long-term Treasuries advanced as oil prices snapped a three-day rally, aiding the US inflation outlook ahead of Wednesday’s release of September consumer prices data.

Ten- to 30-year US government debt yields were two to three basis points (bps) lower on the day, maintaining their war-driven connection with oil prices, where US benchmark West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude futures had pared a 2.2% drop to less than 0.5%. It was the Treasury market’s first trading day since Friday, even as US stock trading took place during Monday’s US bank holiday.

Meanwhile, short-term Treasury yields were 2bps to 3bps higher on the day after erasing declines. They stabilised as expectations for another Federal Reserve interest-rate hike by the end of the year stayed intact. The performance of US stocks remains in focus following last week’s record high for the S&P 500, and semiconductor shares and the Nasdaq 100 pared their initial response to a slump in Asian equities led by Korean chipmakers.

“Geopolitics, AI and rates remain the main themes driving markets,” said Mohit Kumar, chief economist and strategist for Europe at Jefferies.

Stock investors are turning cautious on the artificial intelligence (AI) trade, one of the hottest corners of the market this year, heading into earnings season. Rising competition, stretched valuations and concerns over soaring AI spending have raised questions about whether companies can deliver results that justify the sector’s breakneck rally. A poll by Bank of America Corp showed investors are the most exposed to technology stocks since the Covid pandemic in 2020.

See also: DayOne in early talks with banks for potential US$500 mil bond — Bloomberg

The US benchmark 10-year yield hit 5.36% last week, the highest since 2002, amid growing worries over the nation’s fiscal deficits and as elevated oil prices boosted bets on Fed hikes. Rising global borrowing costs have fuelled concern about economic growth, increasing scrutiny over equity valuations.

US inflation gauges, while far below their 2022 peak levels, have been reinvigorated by rising oil prices since the US attacked Iran in late February, disrupting Middle East supply. The Fed’s favoured inflation gauge was 3.4% in August and has exceeded the 2% target level since 2021. A separate gauge, the US consumer price index, also was 3.4% in August and will be updated for September on Wednesday.

Economists in a Bloomberg poll expect a 3.6% CPI reading overall and 2.5% excluding food and energy, up from 2.4% in August.

See also: Treasury 10-year yield hits highest since 2002 on rate outlook

St Louis Fed president Alberto Musalem last week signalled interest rates should increase over the next six-to-nine months, while his Cleveland counterpart Beth Hammack said on Monday that smaller, more frequent adjustments to policy can help inflation expectations remain anchored. Minutes of the Fed’s September policy meeting showed last week that all 19 officials backed the decision to raise interest rates.

Despite Tuesday’s decline, the prospect of higher yields remains a concern for bond investors, who are also assessing the potential impact from President Donald Trump’s deal on Russian diesel supplies, alongside the outlook for US monetary policy.

A surge in government bond yields is the biggest emerging risk to the global financial system, according to Athanasios Vamvakidis, deputy director at the capital markets division of the International Monetary Fund.

Tuesday’s stock losses in Asia followed a selloff in technology shares on Wall Street that left a US gauge of chip stocks at its weakest since mid-September.

title: S&P 500 holds firm as banks report earnings, chipmakers slump
article:
(Oct 13): US stocks were little changed Tuesday despite a deepening sell-off in chipmakers, as traders sorted through generally strong results from JPMorgan Chase & Co, Goldman Sachs Group Inc and other lenders in the start to third-quarter corporate earnings season.

The S&P 500 Index was up less than 0.1% as of 9.56am in New York, hovering near a fresh record. The Nasdaq 100 Index fell 0.3%, as a sell-off in chipmakers extended for another day. Makers of hard-disk drive components were hit the hardest, with Seagate Technology dropping as much as 7.9% while Western Digital Corp slumped 5.5%.

“Banks are still willing to lend, spreads are narrowing, and companies are asking for more credit despite elevated rates,” wrote Jeffrey Roach, chief economist at LPL Financial. “Inflation and geopolitical risks could still cloud the outlook, but companies appear willing to look past some of the uncertainty when growth opportunities are good enough.”

China’s CXMT is narrowing the technology gap with Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix Inc and Micron Technology Inc — the world’s biggest memory chipmakers — raising the prospect of greater competition that could erode the three DRAM giants’ pricing power and market share. Micron and US-listed shares of SK Hynix both slid about 5%. Sandisk Corp was off 3.8%. Nvidia Corp and Broadcom Inc were each down less than 0.5%. Advanced Micro Devices Inc fell 2.2%.

Among other individual stocks, JPMorgan Chase — up just 3.8% this year through Monday — rose 1.7% to erase an earlier loss, after the bank boosted its net interest income forecast for the full year. Goldman Sachs climbed 1.7% after its equities traders blew past expectations in the third quarter. US banking stocks are already in a correction, with the KBW Bank Index down 11% from its mid-August peak.

Citigroup Inc’s fixed-income traders handed in their best third quarter in at least a decade, while Wells Fargo & Co reported quarterly earnings that topped Wall Street estimates as consumers and businesses held steady. Citigroup slipped 0.3% and Wells Fargo fell 0.6%.

See also: Goldman’s equity traders post big haul as credit, rates miss

Corporate America is navigating one of the strongest profit cycles in recent history. Yet investors are growing uneasy about whether massive AI spending will pay off, especially as a higher cost of capital raises the hurdle rate for investment.

Negative headlines — including a warning on issues with funding the AI buildout and ‘casino’-like market sentiment from Broadcom chief executive officer Hock Tan — come at a time when investors have piled into the trade. That said, other nooks of the AI trade were stable Tuesday, with Apple Inc, Microsoft Corp and Alphabet Inc all rose.

Fund managers in Bank of America’s latest survey are the most exposed to technology stocks since the rebound from the Covid pandemic six years ago, with 37% overweight the sector. About 45% of respondents agreed that there will be an AI bubble in 2027, while 42% don’t see a bubble.

See also: Johnson & Johnson mulls spinning off orthopedics business as medtech sales disappoint

But nothing seems to faze traders lately. The S&P 500 hasn’t posted a 1% decline in 52 trading days through Monday. If the trend continues through Tuesday’s closing bell, it would mark the longest such stretch since January 2020, data compiled by Bloomberg show.

Oil prices slipped, with Brent crude declining to around US$105 a barrel even though tensions in the Middle East remain high. That is still higher than roughly US$72 per barrel in late February, before the Iran war. Energy shares were among the best performing groups in the S&P 500, rising nearly 1%, with ConocoPhillips and ExxonMobil Holdings Corp both climbing less than 1% apiece.

The latest report on the consumer price index is due on Wednesday, followed by the producer price index on Thursday. The S&P 500 is projected to swing 0.75% in either direction on Wednesday, options-market data compiled by Citigroup Inc show.
• Domino’s Pizza Inc fell 4.8%, on pace for its largest decline since June, after the restaurant chain reported total domestic stores comp sales growth for the third quarter that missed the average analyst estimate.
• Of note, Johnson & Johnson fell 4.1% — on track for its biggest drop since April 2025 — after reporting more anaemic growth in the company’s medical device business, though it raised its profit guidance thanks to demand for newer drugs in cancer and autoimmune diseases. Meantime, UnitedHealth Group Inc rose 2.5% on an upbeat outlook.
• Elsewhere, Syndax Pharmaceuticals Inc plunged 14% — heading for its worst day since May 2025 — after the biotech said a phase 2 trial of axatilimab failed to meet its primary endpoint of annualised rate of decline in forced vital capacity in a rare lung disease.
• VF Corp jumped 5% after Piper Sandler and Truist Securities upgrade the retailer to buy-equivalent ratings, noting the company’s Vans brand is at an inflection point.

title: US existing-home sales edged up ahead of mortgage-rate shock
article:
(Oct 13): Sales of US existing homes rose in September for the first time in four months, although a surge in mortgage rates and high prices are set to keep activity depressed through the remainder of the year.

Contract closings climbed 1.5% last month to an annualised rate of 3.99 million after a downward revision to August sales, figures released on Tuesday by the National Association of Realtors (NAR) show. That topped the 3.95 million median estimate of economists surveyed by Bloomberg.

 

Despite the increase, “August and September marked the two slowest months for home sales this year,” NAR chief economist Lawrence Yun said in a statement. “Further increases in mortgage rates in recent weeks mean fewer buyers can qualify to purchase a home.”

At least some of last month’s modest improvement predated the more than half-point climb in mortgage rates since early September to 7.49%. September’s gain also belies the formidable challenges facing the nation’s housing market.

Earlier in the year, the country had been making some progress in reducing the so-called “lock-in” effect — the disincentive to move that homeowners face because of their low existing borrowing costs.

However, the recent surge in rates has halted that progress. It also adds a “US$19,000 shock” for would-be buyers with a US$2,000 monthly budget, Realtor.com chief economist Danielle Hale said earlier this month in a blog post.

See also: US small-business optimism falls on dimmer economic outlook

“The reset in rates over the last five weeks has shaved a little more than 6% off of the purchasing power of buyers across every budget, which is almost twice the typical price-savings advantage of buying in this less competitive season,” Hale said.

Higher financing costs are likely to weigh on prices if they’re sustained. In September, the median sales price rose 1.3% from a year ago to US$417,500, NAR data show, extending a run of year-over-year price increases dating to mid-2023.

Meantime, the supply of previously owned homes for sale climbed 4.6% from a year ago to 1.6 million, NAR data show. That represents 4.8 months of supply at the current sales pace, staying at the more than decade high it reached in August.

See also: US consumer sentiment falls to five-month low in October

The still-elevated prices and surge in mortgage rates have hurt housing affordability, which is helping fuel the debate over the high cost of living, a central theme of November’s midterm elections. NAR’s housing affordability index, which measures whether a typical family earns enough to qualify for a mortgage for a median-priced home, slipped 1.2% from a year ago.

Previously owned home sales in both the South and the West rose 2.8% in September. Sales in the Midwest were flat and activity in the Northeast fell.

“The fourth-quarter outlook for closing activity will clearly be down, maybe even measurably down,” Yun said on Tuesday on a call with reporters. “We are seeing more delays in the contracts with these rising interest rates.”

title: Goldman’s equity traders post big haul as credit, rates miss
article:
(Oct 13): Goldman Sachs Group Inc’s equities traders blew past expectations in the third quarter (3Q), while its fixed-income and rates-trading counterparts fell far below Wall Street’s estimates.

The company’s equities traders, who in July posted a record of any bank for a third straight quarter, reported revenue of US$6.44 billion for the three months through September, according to a statement on Tuesday. That’s lower than the all-time high, from the second quarter, of US$7.42 billion, but still beat the expectations of analysts compiled by Bloomberg.

Fixed-income and commodities traders brought in US$3.47 billion, significantly lower than expected and an almost 1% drop from a year earlier, after chief executive officer David Solomon warned in September of a slower quarter. The decline reflected heavy slumps in mortgages and credit, as well as lower revenue from interest-rate products, the company said on Tuesday, while currencies and commodities were higher.

Goldman’s dealmaking machine helped drive growth in 3Q, with its investment bankers bringing in a higher-than-expected fee haul of US$3.22 billion. The bank’s asset-management unit also drew record management fees.

Goldman has led the rebound in Wall Street dealmaking while also pulling in billions of dollars from trading around volatile equity and fixed-income markets. Like peers, it’s seen its share price retreat in the face of rising bond yields weighing on capital-markets activity.

On Tuesday, Solomon pointed to “a complicated operating environment” and the “current complexity and uncertainty in the world.”

See also: Johnson & Johnson mulls spinning off orthopedics business as medtech sales disappoint

Goldman shares climbed 2.8% at 9.34am in New York. If the price holds up, a fleet of its top executives are in line for a collective payout in excess of US$500 million later this month.

Pay rose along with the bank’s boost in revenue, pushing compensation and benefits expenses to US$5.12 billion, a 9% increase from a year earlier. Year-to-date, those expenses are up 17% compared with the same period in 2025.

The bank’s incentive fees surged almost eightfold from a year earlier to US$587 million. That was tied to arranging bets for its wealth clients on SpaceX during its early funding rounds, Bloomberg News reported this month. Goldman’s revenue from those fees far surpassed the price it was paid for advising on the record IPO.

See also: NYSE owner plans futures for livestock in a bid to challenge CME Group

Goldman also made two key acquisitions in the quarter to expand its more than US$4 trillion asset-management division. It bought exchange-traded fund provider NEOS Investments for US$2.25 billion and LCN Capital Partners, a commercial real estate investor, for as much as US$410 million.

title: Johnson & Johnson mulls spinning off orthopedics business as medtech sales disappoint
article:
(Oct 13): Johnson & Johnson reported another quarter of anaemic sales in its medical technology division and said it is leaning towards spinning off, rather than selling, its orthopedics business.

Medical technology sales rose just 2.5% in the third quarter, missing estimates and trailing more sizable gains in the company’s larger drug business. Overall revenue was roughly in line with expectations, exceeding analyst estimates by the narrowest margin in years.

“Medtech needs to improve quite frankly,” Chief financial officer Joe Wolk said in an interview. Management are “leaning towards a straight spin” of the orthopedics business as opposed to a sale, he said. “We think that’s the greatest way to create value, and that’s likely the path going forward.”

Bloomberg reported last month that Apollo Global Management Inc was in discussions to buy the division at a valuation close to US$20 billion, though the talks could still end without an agreement.

“This quarter did not materially advance the growth narrative,” RBC Capital Markets analyst Trung Huynh wrote in a note to clients, citing “another lacklustre Medtech quarter.”

See also: NYSE owner plans futures for livestock in a bid to challenge CME Group

J&J’s shares fell 3.7% at 9.32am on Tuesday in New York. They have risen 38% in the past 12 months through Monday’s close, compared with a 19% gain for the S&P 500 Index.

Geopolitical concerns including the conflict in the Middle East and austerity measures in some European countries have hit overseas sales of devices, Wolk said, among other issues. International medtech sales were largely flat, with surgical devices in particular falling 3.4%.

Medical devices results are weak “really across the board,” Mizuho analyst Jared Holz said in a note to clients, noting that’s “the area of most scrutiny today”.

See also: S&P 500 hovers near all-time high before earnings

While J&J’s pharmaceutical business is about twice the size of its medtech business in terms of revenue, issues at the latter have preoccupied investors of late. Last quarter, the medical device unit came in slightly below estimates due in part to weakness in the Abiomed heart pump business.

The company raised its profit guidance as demand for newer drugs in cancer and autoimmune diseases overshadowed the disappointment with medical devices. It now expects adjusted earnings for the full year to be in the range of US$11.05 to US$11.15 a share, up from a prior view of US$10.96 to US$11.11. The midpoint of the new range is above analyst projections.

As the first major pharmaceutical company to report each quarter, J&J’s performance is viewed as a harbinger for the sector. Tuesday’s results suggest that drugmakers are successfully navigating changes in federal policy as well as leadership turnover at the US Food and Drug Administration.

Revenue in the pharmaceutical business rose 7.7% from a year earlier, compared with 2.5% gains for the medical device unit.

Highlights in the quarter included 68% sales growth for Tremfya, a newer autoimmune drug that topped analyst estimates. Sales of the psychiatric drug Caplyta soared 66% as prescriptions for newer uses started to kick in, including add-on therapy for depression.

Tecvayli, used to treat the bone marrow cancer multiple myeloma, saw sales rise nearly 77%. J&J’s top-selling Darzalex, also for multiple myeloma, grew at a double-digit clip but fell short of analyst estimates.

Although the company doesn’t yet break out sales for its new psoriasis pill Icotyde, Wolk said that 20,000 people have been prescribed the drug.

In the devices segment, J&J is focusing on faster-growing areas. In July, it got a foothold in the hot robotic surgery market with FDA clearance for its Ottava soft-tissue robotic surgical system.

title: ICE plans futures for livestock in a bid to challenge CME Group
article:
(Oct 13): Intercontinental Exchange Inc (ICE), owner of the New York Stock Exchange, is planning to offer contracts for betting on future cattle and hog prices, competing with longtime incumbent CME Group Inc as it moves its systems to the cloud.

 

The first cattle and hogs futures contracts will be listed before the end of the year, targeting a Dec 7 launch, according to ICE executives. The exchange operator will offer physically settled cattle futures, as well as three cash-settled contracts for cattle and hog prices, all pending regulatory review.

CME, the largest US futures exchange, is moving its matching engine for certain instruments to a new Google Cloud data centre. In response, ICE is looking to shake up the industry by providing another option to hedge.

“We received significant inbound customer demand from those seeking credible alternatives to what has historically been a singular choice for cattle,” Trabue Bland, ICE’s senior vice president of futures markets, said in a statement.

The debate over CME’s move to the cloud has intensified among trading firms and the agriculture community since the exchange announced its plans for the new system, which was slated to be located in Dallas, according to people familiar with the matter who asked not to be identified discussing a private matter. Some firms have expressed concern that the shift might increase costs and slow trading speeds, two of the people said.

Chicago-based CME, which has offered cattle and hog trading since the 1960s, has previously said that moving its tech infrastructure to the cloud can help it control costs, create real-time analytical capabilities and increase efficiencies. Outgoing chief executive officer Terry Duffy has said he would not put products in the cloud unless they are “better than what I have today.”

CME said on Monday in a statement that a previously disclosed move of its livestock markets to Dallas won’t have to go along as planned, since a newly built data centre in Aurora, Illinois, is coming online faster than expected.

See also: Asian stocks drop as oil stokes inflation worries

Dallas will still have a disaster recovery facility, but the interim move of the primary market will no longer be required, a company representative said.

CME has contracts for both younger feeder animals and mature live cattle that are ready for processing. Those futures prices have skyrocketed in recent years as the US’s herd shrank to its smallest size in over half a century, pressuring margins for meat processors and some ranchers.

See also: Temasek CIO says AI, inflation pose biggest market risks in 2027

A measure of volatility for the most-active live cattle contract peaked in late 2025 and has remained elevated since, prompting some traders to exit the market. Aggregate open interest, meanwhile, dropped in August to its lowest levels in over two years, and has only modestly recovered since.

Managing beef prices has been a key focus for restaurants and retailers, as the protein remains an outsize driver of food inflation. Stores have trimmed serving sizes, turned to cheaper cuts or promoted other proteins, while the Trump administration has been trying to boost foreign supplies in an effort to tamp down prices.

Exchanges in the US and abroad are racing to list products that give investors new ways to hedge risks. CME has listed new instruments for protecting against price movements on livestock items such as beef. ICE is sending out a notice to members this week to announce its new, alternative contracts, which will be listed under the codes COW, MOO and SOW.

“There are moments in time in the evolution of markets where choice becomes a compelling motivation, and we believe this is an inflection point for the industry as we work to launch a cattle futures market,” Bland said.

title: Citigroup fixed-income traders post higher revenue in 3Q as rivals miss
article:
(Oct 13): Citigroup Inc’s fixed-income traders handed in their best third quarter (3Q) in at least a decade, beating analysts’ expectations and sending the bank’s revenue for the period to one of its highest levels ever.

Desks handling bonds, currencies and commodities reeled in US$4.4 billion, topping the US$4.3 billion average of analyst expectations, according to a statement on Tuesday. That accompanied a standout quarter for its services business, which helps companies and governments move and manage their money and saw revenue rise 15% on last year to US$6.6 billion.

The better-than-expected results from FICC trading and services helped offset a more sluggish quarter from Citi’s business advising clients on mergers and acquisitions, where revenue declined 4%. Revenue from debt underwriting slipped, too.

Shares edged lower in premarket trading on Tuesday, falling 0.4% as of 8.30am New York time.

Shareholders are watching fixed-income trading desks closely for signs that one of the industry’s biggest profit engines may start to stall amid rising interest rates and a slowdown in mergers and acquisitions. Citi’s fixed-income franchise is Wall Street’s second largest, making it an especially important part of the firm’s broader markets lineup, in which results from some other units were mixed.

So far, the bank seems to be navigating that turmoil better than its rivals. JPMorgan Chase & Co reported earlier on Tuesday a surprise drop in fixed-income trading revenue in 3Q, the first such decline in more than two years. At Citi, the results were led by gains in its credit financing desks within its spread products unit, while rates trading revenue declined.

See also: Thai finance chief runs on four hours of sleep, vitamin IV drips

Chief executive officer Jane Fraser has been pushing the New York-based bank to eke out better returns, making the case to investors that it can increase revenue, keep a tight hold on expenses and narrow the gap with Wall Street peers after years of stagnation. The bank’s shares are up 13% this year, more than all of its major rivals.

Citi reported earnings per share of US$2.85, surpassing the US$2.65 average estimate from analysts tracked by Bloomberg. Revenue rose about 8% to US$23.8 billion, outpacing the US$23.7 billion average estimate.

The bank has been targeting a 10% to 11% return this year to bring profitability closer to peers. Return on tangible common equity amounted to 12.6% in the first nine months. In September, finance chief Gonzalo Luchetti told investors the bank was on track to surpass the 11% figure for the year.

See also: BIS frets about leverage after Situational Awareness emergency

The bank spooked some investors in July, saying it would pull forward some expenses through deeper job cuts and technology investments in the latter half of the year. But the firm was able to keep a lid on costs in 3Q with non-interest expenses totalling US$14 billion. Analysts estimated US$14.4 billion.

Citi is also preparing for a public listing of Banamex, its Mexican consumer-banking business. The firm has lined up banks to advise on the offering in the coming months, when it will offload much of its stake as the tail end of a yearslong strategy under Fraser to downsize retail business outside of the US.
